speechtext: He argued both ways.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) suggests that the Prime Minister left a couple of doors open by which he might leave. I do not want to get off my thought.
If I were to go outside the House of Commons, I might quote Professor W. P. M. Kennedy, of the university of Toronto. His Constitution of Canada has been quoted before in this house. He is considered one of the best constitutional authorities in this country, and I should like to quote from page 452 of that book:
Once the imperial government declares war, Canada is at war, and once a foreign state declares war against Great Britain, Canada is at war. In either case, Canada need not fight, need not supply a man or a ship or assist in any way. Canada might be prepared to preserve the most meticulous neutrality, but as international law now stands, Canada would be at war, and its territory and citizens liable to attack.
And at page 540 he says:
It remains as true in 1937 as it did in 1914 that when the crown is at war, Canada is legally at war.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who is the author?

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: W.P.M.Kennedy, professor of law, university of Toronto.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I knew him well.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He and Mr. Schlosberg wrote another book on the constitution of South Africa, and I quote from page 484 as follows:
With regard to the right of a dominion to remain neutral while the rest of the empire is at war, it is sufficient to state that when the king declares war, all his territories and

dominions are at war. There is no recognition of the divisibility of the legal position of the king.
General Jan Smuts took the same position, namely, that the crown is not divisible. I repeat that those who feel there should be neutrality should come out frankly and declare for independence. I have another quotation here which appeals to me a great deal because it comes from a part of the empire which in a sense has declared its independence. Prime Minister Eamon de Valera of the Irish Free State, now called Eire, declared, according to a dispatch dated February 17, a little over six weeks ago, that " Eire could not remain neutral in a war between Great Britain and another state." He went on to say:
In the event of a war, it is essential for the economic position of Eire that she should continue her trade with England in cattle and other products. That would undoubtedly be taken to put us in a position of combatants by any nation at war with England, who would think it a vital part of its campaign to prevent food from reaching England.
He goes on:
Its object would then be to bomb our ports and make it impossible for us to carry on our trade. It is to defend our territory against such possible attack that we consider it advisable to bring in increased estimates for defence.
Surely Canada is in exactly the same position as the Irish Free State as to shipping and as to trade, as to supplies of food and as to the possibilities of being attacked.
Then what would we have to do if we were neutral? There are certain duties which devolve upon a neutral by international law, which duties would naturally devolve upon us. I am going to mention three or four of them, and I submit that not one could be carried out by Canada in her dealings with Great Britain if Great Britain were at war and Canada remained neutral. For instance, we could not supply munitions or food as referred to by Mr. de Valera in the quotation I have just given. An enemy would do his best to prevent any food from going to Great Britain, because no country in the world is so vulnerable as Great Britain as to its food supply. Great Britain cannot keep sufficient food supplies on hand to last any great length of time. That was the attempt made in the last war by German submarines, to starve out Great Britain, and if they could have prevented for a period of three weeks ships from entering the ports of Great Britain they would probably have succeeded.
Second, if a British ship, pursued by a powerful enemy fleet, took refuge in Halifax

Foreign Policy-Mr. Manion
harbour, it would either have to get out of the harbour at the end of twenty-four hours or be interned.
Third, British troops could not cross Canada on our railways if Great Britain were fighting in the Pacific.
Fourth, we would have to show strict impartiality between Great Britain and its enemy. But does anybody in this house imagine that Canada could show strict impartiality between Great Britain and Hitler at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is absolutely impossible to conceive of such an attitude on the part of the Canadian people.
Fifth, if a British fleet were outside Halifax harbour we could not supply it with food taken out by some of our own ships.
Finally, there are certain conditions under which we would have to intern British ships and their crews. These are half a dozen examples of different types of action that Canada would have to take were Great Britain involved in a war and we remained neutral. To me the thing is inconceivable; it is not possible; and therefore again I say that as I understand the situation, neutrality is impossible for us. In other words, when Great Britain is at war, Canada is at war, with the degree of our participation left to the parliament of Canada.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Nor is it desired.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
One of my colleagues
suggests that it is not even desired by any great body of our people in Canada, and I believe that is true.
I come now to another phase of the question, our participation in wars outside Canadian territory. There are some facts that we should remember when discussing this contingency. Canada is not the same type of country as New Zealand or Australia, whose populations are racially compact, that is, compact not in occupation of area but in their nationality. They are practically a uniform people so far as nationality is concerned. In Canada, on the other hand, we are in much the same position as South Africa in that we have different races, a widespread territory, and widely separated viewpoints among our people. Those are facts, not theories, and it is something we must bear in mind when considering this matter and endeavouring always to hold this country together.
The Prime Minister put on record to-day- and I am pleased that he did-the position taken by the different dominions of the empire
during the crisis of September, and he quoted Mr. Chamberlain in the House of Commons at Westminster-to put it briefly-that none of the dominions had offered more than had Canada at that time. That was the statement put on record this afternoon by the Prime Minister. I have here an authoritative statement made in the South African parliament during the week of March 20 to 27, 1939, which was just after the last crisis. I quote it, not to reflect in any sense upon South Africa, but rather to show that South Africa, divided as to race as Canada is, is in the difficult position of endeavouring to hold the country together, just as we are, and the attitude it took was certainly no stronger than that taken by the government here; indeed, I think not so strong. But perhaps I had better read it without comment and leave hon. members to draw their own conclusions. This is the policy of South Africa, as declared in parliament during the week of March 20 to 27 last:
The policy oft the union has always been and will be to live in peace with other nations and to safeguard the peace of the union. Our attitude to-day is still peaceful relationship with everyone. In regard to the present events in central Europe-
This was three or four days after Czechoslovakia had been taken over.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is this General Hertzog's statement?

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is the official declaration to the parliament of South Africa in the week of March 20 to 27. It goes on:
In regard to the present events in central Europe it will be in the interests of the union to remain disinterested. When, however, the activities of any European country assume such nature and proportion as to justify conclusions that their aim is domination over other free countries and peoples and that also the freedom and interests of the union are threatened the time will have arrived for the government to warn their people and to request parliament to give attention to European affairs. In this sense the time for such interference has not yet arrived.
That wholly agrees with the statement made by the Prime Minister this afternoon in regard to the other dominions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What is the source of that?

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am quite sure that it is the official statement made in the parliament of South Africa. I cannot tell just where I got it. I got it from someone whom I do not care to mention. But it is a public statement, an absolutely official statement made by the government of South Africa in the parliament of South Africa during the week March 20 to 27. I believe it was published in the press.

Foreign Policy-Mr. Manion

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It was in the New York Times of Sunday last.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That confirms what I say. Another interesting extract dealing with this very point is from Professor W. P. M. Kennedy's book, The Constitution of Canada, where at page 543 he makes this observation:
Canada is not only a federation but an exceedingly delicately balanced one; and it is well, in the tremendous world in which we live, to remember with something of the practical wisdom so dear to the Greeks, that this delicate situation exists, that foreign policy is ultimately a projection of domestic policy, that the final awful decision of war is npt a fit subject for division on purely party lines, and that there is wide room for differences of opinion without such question-begging epithets as "disloyalty" or "traitor."
That is a very wise observation. If we are to hold the Dominion of Canada together we must realize the facts that I have been pointing out, and we must learn to tolerate the viewpoints of those who do not agree with us. There are in this dominion at the present time two extreme viewpoints on participation in war. There is the extreme view that we should, that we must, participate in all the wars of Great Britain to the last man and the last dollar, without question or discussion. That is condensing the viewpoint to a definite statement, but I think I am stating it fairly. The other extreme view is that we must participate in no war unless we are directly attacked.
These are two extreme viewpoints, diametrically opposed, and I think I have put them fairly: first, that we must participate to the last dollar and the last man. That is what I would call, not offensively, the ultra-British attitude, an attitude more British than Britain herself takes. Those who hold that view rightly point out the value of our _ empire connection, the fact that Great Britain is to-day in a position to defend our trade routes and protect our shores, that we are in a word, as expressed a year ago in this house by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie), dependent for our defence on Great Britain. Then there is the other extreme viewpoint, that we should not participate in any war unless we are directly attacked. Those who maintain that position point out that we have three thousand miles of sea between us and Europe, and a greater distance from any possible menace on the Pacific; that the United States would help us; that we lost sixty thousand men in the last war besides the great number of wounded and crippled; that we incurred heavy debts and pension charges; that the ideals of "a war to preserve democracy " and " a war to end war " have been shattered; that we have, as was expressed 
this afternoon by the Prime Minister in connection with another matter, half a continent to develop, and that we should like to develop it in peace. Therefore they say that we should take no participation at all in the wars of Great Britain. Yet, so far as I know, they all want to remain within the empire.
Let me say that I abhor war as much as they, indeed as much as any man or woman in this great dominion of ours. No one can abhor it more than I do. But, Mr. Speaker,
I am a realist. I believe in the empire.
I believe in its civilization. I believe in its toleration of the many races and creeds which are a part of that empire. I believe in its liberties, parliamentary and personal. I believe in its traditions and institutions. I say, sir, that so long as we are part of that empire, Britain's enemies would consider us at war, and attack us; and I repeat what I have already said and what others have said, that the whole matter is decided by the enemy.
Considering all these facts, and remembering the strong views held iby both extreme sides, I see a very grave danger to the dominion unless some fair compromise policy is adopted. It seems to me that persistence in either of these extreme views, to the ignoring of the very large group who have the other extreme view, means the disruption of Canada, possibly civil war in case there was an international war in which Britain Was engaged, perhaps the ultimate break-up of the British empire. In the last war the conscription of men to go to the front caused violent racial antagonisms, much disharmony, bitterness and misunderstanding-conditions from which as yet we have not wholly recovered; and on top of that I believe I am expressing the opinion of authorities when I say that it was of no real military value so far as the empire was concerned. Not long ago I made it my business to ask an outstanding military authority how mlany men got into the line from Canada through conscription. He said that there were no absolutely authentic or indisputable figures, but he estimated the number at the outside as 10,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I made the same inquiry.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And the right hon. gentleman got the same figures?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am glad to know that,
because it supports my position. The recruitment of 10,000 men out of the half million

Foreign Policy-Mr. Manion
Canadians who went overseas shows that, with all the ill effects conscription had in our country, it exercised but a small effect upon the war.	.
On the other hand, neutrality, or independence, or even failure to cooperate with Great Britain, is as repugnant to a large section of Canadians as is conscription to another large section. It seems to me, therefore, that we must adopt a sane middle course in order to preserve a united Canada and, indeed, to maintain this empire. The policy that I suggest is the one which I gave three days ago in an interview: first, that there should be no conscription of Canadians to serve outside the borders of Canada; second, that we should have full cooperation with the British empire short of the conscription of men to serve outside our borders. We should fully cooperate by means of-for example

volunteer units, whether air forces or any other units which voluntarily choose to go. I mention particularly air forces because some months ago another outstanding military authority in Canada, who held an important position overseas during the great war, told me that at the end of that war almost forty per cent of the whole air force of the empire consisted of Canadians.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Seventy-five per cent.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That would make my
argument very much stronger, but I should not like to adopt that figure; I quote what he gave me. But even forty per cent coming from the Dominion of Canada would be a huge proportion, considering the population of the empire. It was pointed out to me at that time, and I believe the fact is admitted in view of the magnificent records of so many Canadians in the Royal Air Force, that Canadians have a special aptitude for that arm of the service. We can also cooperate by acting as a training ground for Great Britain and, if desired, for other parts of the empire; by supplying munitions, food and so forth, and by fully protecting our own territory.
In regard to conscription, Mr. Chamberlain's view is indicated in a dispatch dated March 29 from London to yesterday's Ottawa Evening Journal, as follows:
The strength of Great Britain's territorial army will be raised to 340,000 officers and men, it was announced in the House of Commons to-day by Prime Minister Chamberlain.
. At the same time the Prime Minister turned his back on conscription and pinned his faith to the voluntary system to get the men needed for the territorial field army which now numbers 130,000 on peacetime establishment.
So we have the British example to follow, as well. I could quote, although I shall not
71492-154J
do so at length, the proceedings of the imperial conferences of 1923 and 1926, in which is emphasized what is the chief duty of each of the dominions, of each part- of the empire.
The primary responsibility of each portion pf the empire represented at the conference for its own local defence.
Perhaps I had better quote the previous few paragraphs to put the statement in its proper sequence:
At the imperial conference of 1923, a resolution on defence was passed, of Which the following is a part:
1.	The conference affirms that it is necessary to provide for the adequate defence of the territories and trade of the several countries comprising the British empire.
2.	In this connection the conference expressly recognizes that it is for the parliaments of the several parts of the empire, upon the recommendations of their respective governments, to decide the nature- and extent of any action which should be taken by them.
3.	Subject to this provision, the conference suggests the following as guiding principles:-
_ (a) The primary responsibility of each portion of the _ empire represented at the conference for its own local defence.
In 1926, after discussion of the defence policies with the different parts of the empire, the conference went on record as reaffirming the resolutions adopted at the last session, the imperial conference of 1923 from which I have just quoted.
I have other reasons for thinking it is improbable that an expeditionary force on anything like the scale which existed in the last war will ever again be expected of Canada. I am going to take the liberty of quoting the words of the Prime Minister himself, who, in a speech on March 25, 1937, spoke as follows:
I may be entirely wrong, but I doubt very much if the British government itself will ever send another expeditionary force to Europe. I think it is extremely doubtful if -any of the British dominions will ever send anotber expeditionary force to Europe. Were war to come on suddenly, I think we would find that the conditions of a world conflict would be so different from what they were in the last war, that anything in the nature of expeditionary forces to be sent from one continent to another would occasion a good deal more than second thought.
My thought is that the Prime Minister surely based this statement on some information given him by Great Britain, because neither he nor I can claim to be an expert, and I assume he must have had some authority for making such a statement as that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
British ministers said the same thing a couple of years ago.

Foreign Policy-Mr. Manion

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Prime Minister points out that some of the British ministers said the same thing. I believe that is correct, but I thought the Prime Minister had, perhaps, more confidential advice than what was said on that matter by some members of the British cabinet. However, I am quoting his words. I could also quote the statement of the former Prime Minister, Mr. Bennett, on his recent western tour. He expressed exactly the same opinion in one of his speeches at some point in the western country. He also must have had some authority for making such a statement. At any rate, the statement has been made by two prime ministers of Canada. I have been told by a number of military authorities that expeditionary forces such as we had in the last war are not expected and probably are not wanted by Britain.
Finally-and I think this has been overlooked-it strikes me that we may need our own men in Canada if we should be attacked, as we might be, on either the east or the west. It is conceivable that Great Britain might be so thoroughly engaged in defending herself that she could not offer us assistance. It is true that under the Monroe doctrine, enunciated over a hundred years ago, the United States took the position at that time that no other European country should be allowed to take possession of any part of this continent. It is also true that President Roosevelt, speaking at Queen's a few months ago, took the position to which the Prime Minister referred this afternoon. Therefore it is true that we might expect support from the United States. But who knows what enemies might combine against both Britain and the United States? We know to-day of the power of three great countries which have a triangular arrangement-Germany, Italy and Japan-and even if Great Britain were not conquered we might be attacked on east and west and might need all our defence forces in the dominion. Some weeks ago I quoted in the house a statement by a congressman in the house of representatives at Washington. He said, "Americans are safe only so long as England and France stand"; "that the British and French democracies are a major bulwark for the United States"; and he added that "the United States first line of defence is Great Britain and France."
Surely, if that is the feeling-and I think we may conclude that it is-of thoughtful American people, it must be to a still greater degree the feeling of the people of our country, no matter from what section or race or creed they spring. It illustrates the change of opinion to which I referred in my open-
ing remarks this afternoon-the remarkable change of opinion that has been taking place throughout the world, particularly in the last four or- five years since the rise of Hitler.
Could anyone imagine a greater change of opinion than the quotation which I have just given demonstrates as having taken place in the minds of the people of the United States in the past few years? That that change is general is obvious to anyone familiar with opinions in the United States. It is demonstrated continually by President Roosevelt and those who speak for him.
In my opening words I pointed out the remarkable change in public opinion, not only in Canada but in Britain and all the democracies, since the rise of the world-menacing Hitler. I suppose I shall be taunted with having changed my viewpoint in regard to these matters. I admit frankly that I have, as have all other thoughtful men in the world to-day, in view of these epoch-making, world-shaking events in the midst of which we live. Indeed, everyone who is at all familiar with the menacing actions of the dictator countries to-day must alter his viewpoint on many matters, or be indeed immune to change. Circumstances are so vastly different to-day from what they were, even four or five years ago, that all of us must recognize the need of change.
In addition, therefore, to the suggested policies which I have outlined, I say that we must also have adequate home defences to defend our own territory and to maintain our institutions. It is regrettable that such huge sums should be spent on destruction instead of construction, but world conditions and national danger demand it.
There should be as well an understanding with the United States and cooperation with that country, because they face the same dangers that we do, except that they are more powerful, and less vulnerable geographically. Anyone can see that who cares to examine the distances between the United States and possible enemies on both east and west. They have greater riches and, for that reason, greater defences. Finally, the United States would not begin to be the prize that Canada would be to a world-dominating dictator of a congested country such as any of those of which we might think.
I am not an alarmist. I am a realist. I believe it is necessary to face the facts. Moreover, there should be, as I said in this house some days ago, a united front of all democracies against world domination by dictators in order to preserve our parliamentary and personal liberties, our free British insti-

Foreign Policy-Mr. Woodsworth
tutions, our very national existence; and to help the empire and other democracies to do likewise. That, it seems to me, is the surest way to preserve world peace.
This is a time when the sane course is also the only course open to us, and when, at the same time, it is the patriotic course for all of us to take.
One closing thought which I have expressed before is this. If we ever again have to participate in any war, all our citizens, whether in the lines or at home, must give their services to this country on the same basis; so that while some offer their lives others must not be permitted to enrich themselves through the tragedy of war.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) will, I am sure, make us all very happy. The Canadian nationalist, the imperialist, the League of Nations collectivist, the pacifist, the isolationist, the North American, the belligerent militarist-each will find some crumbs of comfort in it. I must confess that although I listened carefully throughout the two hours of his speech I really do not know, in the event of war, what action this government would take.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I should have been surprised if my hon. friend had found any comfort in it.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think it is some comfort to me, because I am very much opposed to war, and I am inclined to think that in these circumstances we might keep out. I must also congratulate the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) upon his new type of Toryism. His sturdy Canadianism almost puts the Liberals to shame.	[DOT]
With all the nations, Canada faces a serious international situation which, it seems to me, calls for the clearest thinking of which we are capable. On some things we are all agreed. I believe we are all opposed to war. I do not believe there are any Mussolinis or Hitlers in Canada. We all cling to what we call British traditions and liberty, and we all, I take it, are loyal Canadians. We have a right to differ without having our sincerity questioned.
I would submit in summary form several considerations which must be taken into account in determining our foreign policy. I take it first of all that the maintenance of Canadian unity is perhaps the greatest contribution Canada can make to the peace of the world. We have here two great races and a score of other nationalities whom we have invited to throw in their lot with us. While loyal to Canada, many of these still retain affection for the land of their birth, just as we do. When war comes, it would seem as if all the plagues were let loose. I repeat, we ought to try to maintain our Canadian unity.
Again, Canada's policy need not necessarily be that of Great Britain, certainly not that of the ruling classes of Great Britain. I think that is important. Canada, as a self-governing nation, has a right, I think a duty, to decide upon her own policy. Of this I intend to speak more fully a little later.
The Prime Minister paid tribute to British ideals and institutions, and we all agree with him. I believe that these rather than the British navy have been Great Britain's real strength, and we ought not to be diverted into thinking it-is merely her armed strength that has given her power. As a matter of fact, the British empire was won largely by force and has been maintained largely by force. It may be claimed that our British military expeditions have not been as ruthless as those of certain other great empires. It may be claimed that British rule has been beneficent, but that does not alter the fact that the empire was won largely by force and has been maintained largely by force. In form at least "Britannia rules the waves" is not so very different from "Deutschland uber alles." It ill behooves us to denounce others for using in this day methods not so different from those used by our empire in an earlier day. The Prime Minister said to-day that Great Britain has no territorial ambitions; no, she is one of the satisfied nations; but the struggle between the so-called "have" nations and the "have nots" will continue until the nations of the world learn their essential community of interest, and adopt some kind of cooperative administration.
We thought we had in the League of Nations at least the beginning of a world organization. But alas, the United States withdrew; the great nations would not subordinate their interests or even recognize a supemational authority, and so the league has largely failed. Back then came the world of power politics, power politics dominated by class interests; the result, Manchuria, Ethiopia, Austria, China, Munich, Czechoslovakia, Spain. A leading Britisher said in my hearing not so many weeks ago that the propertied classes in Great Britain feared that republican Spain was too much under the influence of the left, and hence had not opposed Franco,-a revealing point of view. Now Madrid has fallen and there is established a block of authoritarian states. In my judgment the policies of the present

Foreign Policy-Mr. Woodsworth
British government have been a series of blunders. Yet Chamberlain is still at the helm. Why should Canada be dragged in?
Canada must assume her share of responsibility for the existing situation. I think we must admit that we did not take our responsibilities under the league very seriously.
There are other matters. I have a clipping here from London, Canadian Press, dated February 21. Mr. A. Edwards, M.P., in the House of Commons complained that "two days before Hitler threatened to march into Czechoslovakia 400 tons of copper arrived at German ports from Canada." Mr. Edwards assumed that the dominions are as loyal to the empire as Great Britain, and he proposed to have the dominions secretary take the matter up. And here is the comment which came from our revenue department officials on this cbmplaint:
Canada is in the same position in this respect is all other countries with raw materials to sell. The dominion has no embargo against Germany with regard to any product. It has an embargo against shipping munitions to Spain but not to Germany.
This makes me hang my head in shame, and then burn with indignation. A few days ago I urged, and I urge again, an immediate prohibition of the shipment of war materials to Germany and Japan. It is all very well to settle back in smug contentment; I know there are certain administrative difficulties which may be pointed out, but we should try our utmost, as we would have to try if war broke out, to prohibit war materials from going to Germany or Japan.
I also advocated, and advocate again, following the lead of the United States, that we place a supertax on German imports.
Apparently both the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition are opposed to conscription. But I venture to say that if we really became seriously involved in war, conscription would be bound to come.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In what way?

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The same way as last time, we would be forced into it.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I take the
responsibility of my statement.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am not going
to discuss that. I am expressing an opinion. It came before and has come in other countries. If we are seriously involved, conscription is bound to come.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Last time it was largely political.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If conscription
"omes, then conscription should be preceded
(Mr. Woodsworth.]
by conscription of wealth. I do not want that left vague as it was left the other day in that curious resolution passed in the Ontario house; I mean all wealth: bank accounts, investments, factories, mines and so on. We are told, "All that a man hath will he give for his life," but we asked our soldiers to go to the front in the late war; we gave them $1.10 a day to risk their lives, while other Canadians remained here and profiteered. That must never take place again.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This government is going
to correct that.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am not sure.
They are not starting out very well.
Beyond all else is the growing conviction on the part of thousands of our people of the futility and beastliness of war. War settles nothing. It ruins the victor as well as the vanquished.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yet the hon.
member wants to start an economic war against Germany.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Some hon. member interrupts, says I want to start an economic war. I did not say an economic war against Germany; I said we should put a super tax on goods from Germany and we should refuse to send them materials of war. If the hon. gentleman will rise in his place later in the debate and say that is not a sane policy, I think the country will be glad to hear it.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will rise now.
The hon. member is certainly at this moment advocating economic war against Germany.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does the hon. member object to it?

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What I am trying to say is that a growing number of people are becoming convinced of the absolute futility of war, and that armaments are no protection against war. Even at this late hour some other way out must be found. I urge collective peace action among as many nations as can be induced to come in, including of course the United States. I think that even at this late date Canada, small nation as she is, ought to take some steps to throw her influence for the reestablishment of something in the nature of the League of Nations.
Here I should like to put on record the position on foreign policy adopted at the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation national convention of July, 1938:
To bring into being a foreign policy based upon the following objectives and principles:
(a) Canada must free herself from her present commitments (based upon the conception of Canada as a colony rather than as a

Foreign Policy-Mr. Woodsworth
free and self-governing nation) which would automatically involve her in a war to which another member of the commonwealth is a party. At present, in addition to legal ties with the empire which have not yet been clarified, guarantees to Great Britain of naval bases and cooperation in war preparedness make active participation inevitable.
While these conditions continue, the oft repeated promise of the government that "parliament will decide" is meaningless. Canada should declare her right to freedom of action in case of war whoever the belligerents may be. Cooperative Commonwealth Federation therefore urges that all steps necessary to attain such freedom of action be taken immediately.
(b) The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation further emphasizes the fact that the large scale manufacture of armaments in Canada so vitally affects our foreign policy that it should be strictly controlled by parliament and not undertaken at the will of private interests. In order to free Canada from these economic entanglements which lead to war and to prevent profiteering in armaments, we advocate the nationalization of the manufacture of arms, munitions and war equipment.
(e) The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation believes that war is not inevitable even at this date, and that genuine collective peace action may still avert the present headlong rush to war. The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation urges that Canada support and cooperate in any such collective action whose aim is the prevention of war and the peaceful settlement of existing disputes.
(d) If collective action should fail and war break out, the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation believes that our decision as to participation must be based on the determination to keep Canada out of any war whose purpose is really the defence of imperialist interests; recognizing that in the future, as in the past, an attempt will be made to dress up imperialist wars in a guise acceptable to the general public.
I should like to speak for a few moments on Canada's right to decide her own foreign policy. This is along the lines of a resolution which has been on the order paper since the beginning of the session, but which will not be reached. The principle underlying it is the same as that underlying Bill No. 16, in the name of the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson). This proposal has already been discussed by the Prime Minister. I think my own point of view is succinctly stated in the resolution on the order paper, which reads:
Whereas at the imperial conference of 1926, the British dominions were defined as being "autonomous communities within the British empire, equal in status, in no way subordinate one to another in any aspect of their domestic or external affairs, though united by a common allegiance to the crown, and freely associated as members of the British commonwealth of nations";
Therefore be it resolved, that this parliament hereby declares to the other members of the commonwealth and to the world that the power to make a declaration of war binding upon Canada is vested solely in the crown on the advice of its Canadian ministers, and calls upon the government to introduce at the present
session such legislation as may be necessary to give full effect and force to this declaration.
Two years ago I stated my position in these words, as they appear at pages 240 and 241 of Hansard-and I would call these words to the attention of the leader of the opposition who has just been discussing this matter from his own point of view:
Canada should claim at once the right to declare war or peace. I brought this matter up last year. I suggested that Canada is said to be autonomous under the Statute of Westminster, but we are also told that when Great Britain is at war, Canada is at war. It would appear that while Canada has now full control of her own legislation, she has not full control over tile executive functions of government. South Africa by her Status of Union Act and Royal Executive Functions and Seals Act sought to attain such control over her own affairs.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But it is doubtful if she did.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Someone may object that if that policy is carried out it will mean independence. If that is so, then I say, by all means, let us have independence. On the other hand, as one who desires to preserve the British connection, I would suggest quite seriously that it_ is only in so far as we in Canada have effective control over the policies which concern our people, and the other dominions have similar control, that we shall be able to maintain the British commonwealth.
Means must be found to clarify existing anomalies and the dangerous situation which essentially is the result of developing from colonial to national status. I say " dangerous." Let me quote this from one of our imperial statesmen.
London, December 15, (Canadian Press- Havas, French Agency). The British _ empire's voice in foreign affairs would be increased manifold if, for example, Canada had a population of 40,000,000 instead of its present 10.000,000, the Duke of Devonshire, dominion's undersecretary, declared in a speech Wednesday night.
"Battleships, tanks, guns and rifles are no good unless you have men," he declared.
That is the news item. Well, what is the suggestion? It is that we dump immigrants into the colonies, encourage them to breed, and then use them for empire raw material. I suggest that Canada is going to have something to say about that.
I urge further that the present policy is "dangerous," because British imperial or even domestic policy may involve Canada, or even imperil her domestic welfare. The leader of the opposition has suggested that, in his opinion, neutrality is impossible without independence. He would then apparently be willing that Canada should tag along at the tail of all British decisions. Surely that is the very abnegation of representative government. If I were in Great Britain I would have some

Foreign Policy-Mr. Woodsworth
voice in saying who the government of Great Britain would be. Living in Canada I have no such voice. And yet, according to the logic of the leader of the opposition, although my life in Canada may be seriously affected, I must obey whatever decision is made by a government in Great Britain, over whose election I have no control at all.
Further, I said it was "anomalous" because statutes tend to lag behind declared principles. This question was discussed by the British Commonwealth Relations Conference meeting which was recently held in Australia. The principal Canadian paper was prepared by Professor F. R. Scott of McGill university. It has been published under the title "Canada To-day." Mr. Scott said:
The overwhelming weight of authority takes the _ view- that legally the state of technical belligerency is created in the dominion by a British declaration of war.
That is apparently the present situation. We cannot help ourselves. But the Prime Minister of course maintains that Canada will decide. In practice, all that means is that Canada will decide to what degree she will participate. That is very largely a farcical position. We were said to decide whether or not we would have a new king. A special session of parliament was called to decide whether or not we would have a new king- and yet when we arrived in Ottawa we found that we had to take the oath of allegiance to the new king before we were permitted to take our seats in the house to decide whether or not he would be our king. I hope that one of these days we shall get away from some of these legal fictions and openly face facts as they are.
Let me state the legal position as I have it from some of my friends who know more than I do about constitutional law. I quote from a memorandum, but I accept the position taken:	;ffj
Until full control over matters of peace and irar^ affecting Canada is vested in Canada, this lominion cannot be said to be fully autonomous ')r equal in status with Great Britain.
The new constitution of Ireland provides that, except in the case of actual invasion, war shall not be declared and the state shall not participate in any war save by the assent of Dail Eireann, and the British government announced that "they are prepared to treat the new constitution as not affecting a fundamental alteration of the position of the Irish Free State ... as a member of the British commonwealth of nations;"
The Union of South Africa by legislation adopted in 1934 has acquired full internal control over the exercise of the royal prerogative on behalf of the union:
Since the Statute of Westminster Canada also has the right to deal with the royal prerogative over external affairs in any way that the parliament of Canada may desire.

Then, Berriedale Keith in the Journal of Comparative Legislation, 1935, is reported to have said, at page 274, that certain decisions seem to establish that any royal prerogative in respect of a dominion may under suitable legislation, be controlled by that dominion. I am here actually quoting from page 263 of Hansard for 1937.
Then, there is one further quotation from Professor Soott which I should like to give somewhat as an antidote to what was said by the leader of the opposition. Professor Scott said:
The same spirit which made Englishmen behead one king and expel another in the seventeenth century, turned the colonies into autonomous dominions in the twentieth century. Independence of action proved that the dominions were British in spirit, not that they were anti-British. It was failure to recognize their own characteristics when displayed by Englishmen outside England which lost the English their American colonies.
How celebrate the visit of the king and his consort to Canada? It is proposed that he dedicate a memorial to a war which ended twenty years ago when, as a matter of fact, the fear is that the threat of another may prevent his visit? Why not celebrate by asking him officially to declare Canada's coming of age, our entrance upon the full rights and responsibilities of responsible government?
Let me turn to another aspect. We are nominally a Christian nation. Prayers are said daily in this house, I suppose as an acknowledgment of that fact. In the Gazette of yesterday there was a rather striking report of a speech by the Reverend Canon Raven, Master of Christ's College, Cambridge, and chaplain to His Majesty the King. He is reported as saying:
It is impossible to reconcile the teachings of Christianity with modern warfare.
And again:
The world is ripe for a new age of mutual understanding and for an almost world-wide cooperative civilization. If a sufficient lead were given I believe there is sufficient common sense and devotion in the world to follow that lead.
I should like to quote from the record of proceedings of the eighth general council of the United Church of Canada held in Toronto in September, 1938. From the section devoted to Christian principles, I read:
The United Church of Canada, in general council assembled, declares its unchanging conviction that war is contrary to the mind of Christ. We believe armed warfare to be contrary to the spirit and teaching of Christ. As Christians we positively reject war, because war rejects love, defies the will of Christ and denies the work of man. We declare the basic Christian principle of the supreme worth of human personality, the economic inter-

Foreign Policy-Mr. Woodsworth
dependence of the peoples of the world and the inherent oneness of mankind. War is the repudiation of these principles and of love and reason. It is a resort to hatred and violence-to barbarism.
I should like to make one more brief quotation from this document which advocates what amounts practically to civil disobedience under certain circumstances. I quote:
Neither the state nor any other power has the right to compel a person to engage in what his conscience declares to be a sinful act. We pray there may never be a clash of loyalties in this regard, but should there be, we hold with the early church that a Christian must obey God rather than man," for only by so doing can we best serve man.
Perhaps it is not good form to quote a church body in this house.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why not?

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Some people do not consider it to be. However, I venture to do so because I believe that what I have just read is fundamentally sound. It seems to me that we have reached a stage in the development of our civilization where we shall have to take our stand and decide whether war is compatible with Christianity or even with civilization itself. We must remember that history teaches us that many evils were once condoned by the church and once had the full sanction of the state. Take slavery, for example. However, there came a time when both state and church realized that slavery must go. Possibly we have reached the stage where we must decide as to whether war is to be abolished as an instrument of national policy and, indeed, whether war is at all compatible with civilization. I know I shall immediately be asked: If there is a mad dog abroad in Europe, what are you going to do?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) says " hear, hear." Immediately we are swept off our feet. We say we must be prepared to fight the devil with fire. Immediately we must put forth every endeavour to be stronger than he is from the military point of view.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Some hon. members say " hear, hear." I hear that all over the house. That is the accepted view.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If a man attacks me I have to defend myself.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You say so.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Which is only right.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There was one
historical example: one very eminent person who is regarded as being divine who did not think so. You say he perished-yes. But I often think of those lines of James Russeil Lowell:
Truth forever on the scaffold, Wrong forever on the throne,-
Yet that scaffold sways the future, and, behind the dim unknown,
Standeth God within the shadow, keeping watch above his own.
You may say that is absolutely skyJblue idealism.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is what we all believe.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If it is what we all believe, some of us ought to be willing to try to put it into practice.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Surely the hon. member would not be prepared to leave the world to the attacks of a mad dog.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We come back to that every time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend defends himself pretty well when he is
attacked.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He does some attacking too.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He never turns the other cheek.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have never yet carried a gun to defend myself, but perhaps you will say there are police and all that kind of thing. The house laughs, but I am serious about this because I think it is a big issue. I think we shall have to work out this principle in hitherto untried applications. I do not think we can go on as our fathers have done, as all nations have done, and civilization maintain itself much longer. Some other way will have to be found. If the civilization of western Europe is to be reduced to that of ancient Rome and Greece, as may easily be the case, then laboriously and patiently we shall have to rebuild. Why should we not be willing to make for peace some of the sacrifices that are required for war? That is my point. We cannot expect that everything is going to flow along smoothly and we remain smug and content.
I have no use for war, but I confess that I have more respect for the soldier who goes to the front than I have for the man who stays at home and profiteers. I have more use for the nation that goes into war to defend a principle than I have for the craven nation that stays at home simply to keep its hide whole. If as a Canadian nation we are going to take our place in world affairs on



Foreign Policy-Mr. Woodsworth
another basis than that of war, we shall have to be prepared to make at least as great sacrifices as we would if we went into war.
My time is almost up, but before I close I should like to put on the record two or three paragraphs from the recent speech of Mussolini, which I fancy all hon. members have read:
First, as regards the professional pacifists- He is speaking, I take it, not of those whom we regard as pacifists, but rather of those who advocate peace and who have allied themselves so largely with the League of Nations and agencies of that kind.
First, as regards the professional pacifists, they are particularly detestable individuals. And as regards the word peace, it is by now virtually^ worn out from much use and rings falsely like counterfeit money.
Again he says:	.
No matter how things go we wish to hear no more about brotherhood, sisterhood, cousins and such other bastard relationships because relationships between states are relations of force, and these relations of force are the determining elements of their policy.
Again :
We must arm. The watchword is this: More cannon, more ships, more airplanes, at whatever cost, with whatever means, even if it should mean wiping out all that is called civil life.
When one is strong one is dear to one's friends and feared by one's enemies. Since prehistoric times one shout has come down on the waves of the centuries and the series of generations: Woe to the weak!
There you have the doctrine of stark, brutal force.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But what can men of peace do when there are rulers of that kind at large in the world?

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mussolini is correct. Since prehistoric times it has been, "Woe to the weak." We as a race began down in the slime, yet in some way or another we have risen to the stage which we call civilization, and this in spite of the brutes that our ancestors were. The race has risen because there were a few men of each generation who caught a gleam of something greater ahead. There are such things in my judgment as truth and justice and love.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And in my better moments I have the courage to believe that truth will prevail even though there is falsehood on every side.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And I have the courage to believe at times that we shall have justice even though one is almost over-IMr. Woodsworth.!
whelmed by injustices on every side. I never read a book of poetry or attend a fine drama without believing that love has some real force in it and that some day it will touch the hearts even of the hardest. I like to think that. I do not live up to it always, but I like to think it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We all do.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And I say that this creed of Mussolini's is little less than blasphemy.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear. Mr. MACKENZIE KING: We all agree.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And yet the tendency is for us to lower ourselves to his level.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, that is slander.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The tendency is, in my judgment, that we adopt the very means that he is using. We see these authoritarian states set up in power and flourishing like a green bay tree. But they have within them the seeds of decay, and even without the intervention of some outside power they will one day crumble of their own inherent rottenness. But if we set up the same thing, what then? Why, we begin to follow the same course.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, the motive is not the same.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes? Never mind the motive. I would call the attention of the Prime Minister to a book that I have not myself read carefully, Aldous Huxley's Ends and Means. We cannot adopt wrongful means even to gain good ends. Instead of the end justifying the means, the means debase the ends.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is right, but can my hon. friend tell me how those anti-Christian forces are going to be prevented from sweeping over the whole world unless Christian forces array themselves against them?

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not call these
present arrangements such as armaments, Christian forces at all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They are not the forces. The people behind them are the forces.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is it wrong to be armed against bandits?

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think on the whole the police and the soldiers are not nearly so powerful in this world as some people believe. Further, may I say I am firmly convinced that in this scientific world we are learning

Foreign Policy-Mr. Hay hurst
that we are not getting very far in dealing with effects, we must learn-to deal with causes.
I do not know that I am prepared to say we should open every penitentiary and gaol and all that sort of thing. I do not know that I would go that far, although. I do say it seems to me that under our penal arrangements almost as many innocent people suffer as guilty people. But I go further and suggest that two-thirds of the crimes committed could have been, prevented if we had dealt properly with the young people. I firmly believe that; I know I am on good scientific ground, and to the extent to which it is possible I urge that we must begin and keep curative processes at work.
If we are asked, why Hitler? I say unhesitatingly, because of the peace treaty-a victor's treaty. I said that at the time, and I say it again. That was the cause of Hitler. The last time I was in Germany I remember very clearly talking to one of the officials in the department of foreign affairs of the government then in control. As he reviewed the situation in east Berlin, where the communists were rioting, and in Munich, where Hitler was at that time beginning to rise to power, I asked him, "What of the future?" He shook his head and said, "I do not know, but anything is better than this." It was the desperation of the German people, caused very largely by the allies, which, in my judgment, gave birth to Hitler, and we are not going to accomplish very much by going round again in the same old cycle.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I regret to
interrupt, but the hon. member has exhausted his time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Let the hon.
member finish.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I shall be only a
moment, Mr. Speaker. It seems to me that intelligence, idealism, cooperation, if you will, and high moral appeal, are greater in this world even as it is than the application of brute force, and what I would ask of my own nation is that more and more we should think not so much in terms of military defence but rather in terms of the promotion of justice. Here in our own midst we have not justice by any means. Then there is the policy of the good neighbour. We have not followed that by any means. Above all, let us place the higher values of humanity against the greed and the profit-seeking which so frequently dominate our commercial life as well as our international relations.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In following the hon. member for Winnipeg 71492-155i
North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), may I say that there are some things he said with which I agree, and probably some others with which I disagree. When he mentioned brute force,
I thought of the law of the jungle and the remark of students of the science of behaviour, "Make a man sufficiently angry or envious and the dull red eyes of the cave man will glare and stare at you."
I congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) upon the adroitness of his speech this afternoon, a speech which covers pretty well Liberal policy in the field of international relations. We realize that democracy needs leadership, and that the policy of the good neighbour as enunciated by the president of the great republic to the south of us is a good one to adopt at this time. Looking at Europe, we see a great part of that continent, particularly the southeast, in "an atmosphere misty with tears." When the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) was speaking this evening, he mentioned the leader of the Irish Free State. I thought of a story told of Doctor Hyde, president of Eire, At a meeting he attended he was speaking of England, when a man in the audience said, "To hell with England." Doctor Hyde replied, "No, my friend, not 'to hell with England' but 'to heaven with Ireland'." So perhaps, Mr. Speaker, in our discussions we have regarded some of these nations with a certain amount of envy because of the great accomplishments which they have brought about, even under the type of government which they have to-day. When the Prime Minister mentioned that we in Canada should rival them in doing the most for our own people, in giving them more opportunity and greater security, in raising their standards of living, in increasing individual liberty, peace and security to take the place of hate and hysteria, he was comparing Canada and the other democracies with nations which, although labouring under a different type of government, have probably shown more efficiency in some respects than have our own democracies.
So to-day we have a challenge to democracy. We need more people who love liberty, more men of the type of the grandfather of the present Prime Minister. We need reform- Now. The Prime Minister mentioned this afternoon some of the alternatives. He said that in the proceedings of the League of Nations too much stress had been placed on penalties; he mentioned the alternatives of the Pan-American union and of the empire. It is true that to-day we are living in a new age. The security of Britain and the security
Foreign Policy-Mr. Hay hurst

of Canada depend greatly upon our achievements in the field of science and knowledge compared with the accomplishments of other peoples. We are now neighbours of any European nation. Canada is a neighbour of Germany. The range of the aeroplane has outmoded national boundaries-boundaries which, as we have seen them on the map of Europe in the past few years, were drawn in a horse-and-cart age, before mankind became conscious of the power of aeroplanes and modern machinery.
I realize that foreign relations is a great subject, one to be discussed with dignity and fairness. We were therefore delighted to hear some clear-cut statements by the Prime Minister regarding the position of Canada in relation to the empire and the United States, and with regard to conscription. Canada contains many different classes and races. My own constituency probably contains representatives of more different European countries than any other constituency in this great country. Quite a member of letters I receive come from Germans in my district. If the Prime Minister wants to give "happiness and sweet content" to the Canadian people, jealousy and misunderstanding on the part of the English and French-speaking people with regard to our new Canadians, and especially our citizens of German origin, must be removed. Many of these German citizens are excellent farmers and are good citizens of Canada, yet newspapers and sometimes their neighbours criticize them unduly because they happen to be Germans.
While Canada is territorially a large country, to-day it has become quite small. Engraved on the portals of this building are the lines:
The wholesome sea is at her gates,
Her gates both east and west.
And to-day a man can leave the Pacific coast and be in Montreal in twelve hours.
We need more vision if we are to give our Canadian youth of all nationalities the opportunity for which they seek.
In a democracy a person should be able to say without hinderance what he thinks of the government, bearing in mind that the happiness of the individual citizen is a paramount consideration. It will be remembered that Voltaire said:
I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it.
