speechtext:
Foreign Policy-Mr. Hay hurst
Slovaks and Ukrainians, but it was hoped the Czechs would meet the problem as Switzerland had done by setting up states or cantons. This was intended to give the minorities a large measure of home rule, but damnosa hereditas of Austria-Hungary still haunts the world. Czechoslovakia had the example of Austria-Hungary before her, but no attempt was made to set matters right. Instead, the Czechs insisted on being the body in control. This caused a large amount of discontent. The minorities insisted on more autonomy, with the result that the seeds of dissension easily germinated and outside help quickly came. Austria-Hungary never accomplished the task of welding these people together, and it is doubtful if any other power will be any more successful.
A nation cannot be welded together unless it has a common means of discussion, or in other words, a common language, a common heritage. The statesmen who drafted the treaty of Versailles overlooked this fact and consequently created a state which was an economic and geographic and ethnographic mistake. The question now is, have these minorities leaped from the frying pan into the fire? Democracy lives only in a spirit of tolerance and individual freedom. It is tolerance and individual freedom which serve to cement the national aspirations of a people. Democracy develops a spirit of kindliness. It has ever been the claim of autocracies that kindliness is a source of weakness, but the spirit of tolerance which develops the freedom of each individual should develop a kindly feeling towards your neighbour if democracy is to survive.
Originally democracy was a form of direct government as found in city states like Athens. Strictly interpreted, democracy means the rule of the people. Abraham Lincoln defined democracy as government of the people, by the people, and for the people. I do not know that there is any kind of government, whether totalitarian -or whatever else, but is government for the people. The essential question is whether the government is by the people. Democracy believes in the individual; the totalitarian states believe that the individual exists for the sake of the power and glory of the state. The state encourages discipline, obedience, courage and self-sacrifice in an effort to be efficient. In a democracy the state exists to enable every individual to develop his own initiative and his own personality as a member of the community. The creed of the dictator relieves men of the drudgery of hard thinking demanded by democracy. Democracy is the only political method by which economic equality will ultimately be achieved. Construc-

tive criticism is the greatest service a citizen can render any community. Doctor L. P. Jakes said that whereas there is no such thing as governing men, there is such a thing as preventing them from governing themselves. So we believe that we must make democracy work.
The dominant civilization on earth is western in character, but unfortunately there is a great cleavage in this civilization. Some believe that man the individual should be supreme; others, that the state should be supreme. Some believe that man should be free; others, that men's liberties should be subordinated to the state. One side says that the state exists for man; and the other, that man exists for the state. One side believes in democracy; the other, in autocracy. Some say that force will win; others, that morality will win.. Surely free men can be happier than those whose liberties have been taken from them. The freedom of the individual cannot be subordinated to the myth of a living state. Political and personal liberty must be preserved to prevent us from traveling the path towards an insect civilization.
Familiarity breeds contempt. We grumble at our political institutions in this country, when we should be extolling their virtues. We have Canadians in this country who were not brought up in the nurture of our institutions, and when we attack thdse institutions contemptuously we are undermining their loyalty to Canada. Scepticism and cynicism regarding our political life break down our ideals of democracy. We must rally to the fight to preserve the liberties we have. Derision of democratic principles has become common, with the result that people look to communism and fascism. People's sympathies are being driven away from parliamentary methods of government because of an impression of vigour and efficiency and determination of dictators. So we must renew our own confidence in democratic principles if we wish to encourage others to share those principles. Democracy cannot buy peace by selling its conscience. The challenge to democracy must become the challenge of democracy. Even in a democracy personal ambitions appear inevitable. We oppose Marxism, but we must retain the fighting spirit without which no generation, certainly no young generation, considers life worth living.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The introduction of foreign affairs in this debate to-day will do a great deal of good and clarify the situation as far as Canada is concerned. The country expects that all parties in this house will want to see the maximum of

Foreign Policy-Mr. Church
unity and the minimum of criticism on such an important matter as this, in such dark days as these, and especially because Canada is such a difficult country to govern.
The great war showed in this country that all the loyalty is not in one party. All classes of people on the whole did the best they could in the great war. God forbid that we should ever see another one in this country, or ever suffer on our own soil the awful horrors of war which the poor people of some other countries have suffered and are suffering to-day through the dictators. The feeling of some people in Canada is that so far as the mother country is concerned, "We are just as good as you are." But the real sentiment of the Canadian people is that while that may be said, they believe in their hearts and know that all they enjoy in the world to-day of liberty, freedom, and civilization they owe to the mother country for protection. In their hearts they know that to be true.
I have known the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) for many years. I have a very high regard for him and also for the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Manion.)
I believe the statements they made to-day will do a great deal to clarify the situation as far as Canada is concerned. Dispatches were read showing that South Africa, Australia and New Zealand did not speak to the mother country more loyally than Canada. That is the trouble in this country, there is too much lip-loyalty. What is needed in Canada to-day is courage, prudence and leadership. That is the great need to-day of our statesmen and those in control. The fate of our empire, of civilization and of freedom is at stake; the fate of all the dominions and countries the world over is wrapped up in the success or failure of Great Britain. If Britain falls, the world will go down into outer darkness, and Canada in common with all other countries will lose the freedom, liberty and civilization which she enjoys.
This is the fifty-sixth day of this session, and at last the house has an opportunity to discuss the trust reposed in the Prime Minister, as head of the Department of External Affairs, in the administration of Canada's foreign policy. I have read many speeches delivered by the Prime Minister, statements he has made in the house and in other parts of Canada. I have read his statement in Paris, and the statement he made when he arrived at Quebec. At no time in the history of the empire has it been more necessary than it is to-day to stand beside the mother country. After all is said and done, in my humble opinion all the money spent on defence by this country,
defence on the land, sea and in the air, will be wasted and thrown away unless that policy is coordinated and in cooperation with that of the mother country.
The Prime Minister has stated that, should an emergency arise, parliament will decide upon what course the country will take, having in view all the circumstances of the case. He has referred to what the other dominions have done and said along the same line. So far as I can see, there is no declaration in his address such as the great majority of people in Canada would like to see, namely a declaration that we stand behind the mother country. In days now past, Sir John A. Macdonald and Sir Wilfrid Laurier did make statements. Sir Wilfrid said that when Great Britain is at war, Canada is at war also.
As was said this afternoon by both leaders, the dictators are the ones who are going to decide whether or not Canada will be at war. To-day dictatorships have what they call shock diplomacy. Those dictators do not give a country any chance. They take everything by shock, with suddenness, ruthlessly and brutally. We talk about parliament deciding whether or not we should participate in a war. Why, before parliament could sit, before we could get to this building, the dictators could sail up the St. Lawrence and, with modern aircraft, destroy every public utility in Canada before anything was done to stop them. There would not be time to do anything. The idea of waiting to call parliament before deciding on a policy does not appeal to wisdom or judgment of the people of Canada.
In 1914 Sir Robert Borden gave leadership and acted promptly, and the country backed him up. In my opinion it would do so again, under our system of responsible government if the emergency should again arise. With all due respect to the statements which were made to-day, Canada, as I view the situation, still has a policy of isolation. We make our own treaties. Except through the ties of allegiance to the mother country, we are a separate country. I have taken notice of what has been done since 1921 with respect to separatism in this country and a week ago gave a summary of how far we had gone. The very idea of war is hated and detested by everybody; nevertheless preparation is necessary. No one wants war. It is right to hate war, but we have to face the facts. There is at stake the question of the defence of Canada and the empire, and also of our liberty and freedom and the principles of civilization.
In England they have been slow to get started, but now they realize the mistake they made in disarming. They are now rearming.
Foreign Policy-Mr. Church

At Norwich the labour unions voted by
2,500,000	to less than 200,000 for an armed Britain. This has been forced upon Great Britain; she has been compelled to make heavy expenditures on armaments. The government does not want it; the opposition does not want it-nolbody wants all those expenditures of money. But they are necessary, in view of the condition in which the world finds itself to-day. An unarmed Britain only invites insult and invasion and, in the end, extinction. She scrapped the finest army, navy and air force the world ever saw, to please the pacifists.
Adequate armaments are necessary, but adequate armaments without adequate manpower are inadequate. We know by chapter 132 of the Militia Act that the militia can be called out for active service in Canada and also, when advisable, for the defence of Canada. In connection with Canada's stand I should like to see more clarity than we have had in the past. Let us get rid of this metaphysical language about foreign affairs and defence; let the country know plainly what Canada's defence policy is.
Where is Canada? She seems to be at the cross roads on defence policy. Where is she drifting? She seems to be depending for defence on the Monroe doctrine, Pan-Americanism, and protection by the United States fleet in the Pacific and Atlantic. Canada, which was first in the Diamond Jubilee procession of 1897, refused to take any part in protective measures for Great Britain in the Pacific or aid to the Singapore base. She has refused to cooperate with New Zealand and Australia for the protection of the Pacific, or to attend the Pacific conference. All the powers who were interested were at the opening in February, 1938, of the Singapore base or attended the Pacific conference, but Canada was not there. At the opening of the Singapore base Britain, the United States, New Zealand and Australia were represented, but Canada was not there.
It seems to me, if we may judge from what happened yesterday and the day before in the Quebec legislature, that there is something radically wrong with education in this country. May I say that education consists of more than mere book-learning. A man may win a triple first at the university of Toronto, at McGill or at some other university, and yet be uneducated. Conversely, a man may be educated and not be able to read or write. George Stephenson could not read or write when he was eighteen years of aSe, yet he discovered the steam engine and perfected it.
There is something wrong with modern education; there is something lacking. There
(Mr. Church.]
are more important things which should be learned in education, namely service and sacrifice, discipline, love of country, duty to one's country and service to humanity and the cause of freedom. That is one of the weaknesses in Canadian education. May I say that the provocative pacifism which has been going on in this country is something to be deplored. One of the thirty-nine articles of the Church of England, article 37, says that it shall be lawful for Christian men at the commandment of the magistrate to bear weapons and to serve in the wars. Since when has it become a crime for the young people of Canada to defend one's country. Let me say that on many occasions the militia of Toronto has done its duty. They went to northwestern Canada, that section of Canada from which some of the leading pacifists in this house have come-and they saved in 1885 the prairie provinces and Canada from being dislocated. They took a very active part in the northwest rebellion. In my opinion, national service in Canada must be adapted to conditions.
At the opening of the session I asked these questions:
1.	Have any steps been taken by the government to secure a national register for Canada tor delenee or economic or industrial or labour purposes ?
ou, vviictL are
3. Will a census or modern doomsday book, or national register be ordered or compiled of (a) industrial power, (b) economic power, (e) food power, (d) manpower, (e) military and defence power and (f) unemployed?
After a lot of running round I have not yet received a proper reply. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) was the only one who gave a return to my question. There has been no national register. What is being done in Australia with regard to national defence? She is voting two and a half billion dollars for defence purposes over a number of years. She voted for the Singapore base, and for a fleet of warships of her own and union for defence with Britain. She has decided on a compulsory national register of all from fifteen to sixty-four. It may not be for war purposes, but it is necessary. Are we going to wait for another war before we have a national register in Canada? Now is the time for it; do not wait until it is too late, as was done in 1914. Shall we ever have a generation of Canadians who will believe in preparation and avoid the awful sacrifices of 1914? We must remember the terrible situation which we had in 1914 was on account of lack of preparation. I believe national service in Canada must be adapted to the conditions of the times. We should be prepared.

If it is a social and moral duty for love of country to save our dominion, then we may depend that our youth will rise to any leadership. Youth will be ready to admit that they have a duty and an obligation to their country, if they have leadership. The Prime Minister should aid each school board to tell the youth that Canada expects each of them to do his or her duty. Canada is looking for leadership in domestic affairs and in foreign and defence affairs. If we have leaders who will rise to the situation, then they may be sure that Canada will willingly accept any action taken. The youth of Canada will not fight for the league, for appeasement, or in another country, against fascism or communism.
In my _ opinion the greatest mistake the Prime Minister has made is in adopting a policy of silence, in adopting what I consider a policy of provocative silence. Mr. Chamberlain has placed all his cards on the table. He made a statement in the British house the other day because he considered that parliament and the country should know all the facts.
Second, I think the government has failed to collaborate and to coordinate the defences of Canada with those of Great Britain. There should be less of this separatism and pacifism. This government has made one great mistake. It is the worst of all; it has failed to give leadership. It has underestimated the great patriotism of the Canadian people. The problem of defence is a most important one. This whole question has been altered by the improved weapons of attack. There has been a great improvement in aircraft. We have Ethiopia as an example of what can be accomplished in air attacks. A warship could sail up the St. Lawrence fully equipped with aeroplanes and anti-aircraft pompom guns. This is the type of defence that should be provided for.
As I said in a debate in this house on March 24, 1938, on the defence estimates, Abyssinia was recently a theatre of war and we all know the destruction of civilian population that occurred through that means of attack. Abyssinia is an open country with only a small density of population compared with the island of Montreal, the cities of Quebec, Ottawa and Toronto and other parts of Canada. Air raids can work great havoc in time of war, and the menace will be a very real one in Canada, especially to the people of Quebec, the maritime provinces and British Columbia. What are we doing to take care of the civilian population? Nothing. Aircraft could come up the Ottawa river at a moment's notice. I should like to direct the
Foreign Policy-Mr. Church
attention of the Social Credit members to what might happen. An air attack might occur and the whole social credit system be destroyed at a moment's notice. It was not many years ago that a few men from Toronto went out to the northwest and saved the whole prairies for Canada. Aircraft could come up the Ottawa and destroy this building, the railway station and all the public utilities in eastern Canada.
An aerial bombardment is one of the dangers most to be apprehended in time of war, particularly in large cities with their dense populations. The protection of cities from aerial bombardment should be one of the chief objectives of the national defence department, and proper equipment for defence against this menace should be provided. Large quantities of poisonous gas could easily be spread over a large area, as was done in Abyssinia. Incendiary bombs could be dropped on our large cities with great destruction and slaughter, and the enemy aircraft could get back to their base in practically no time. These attacks would not only bring ruin to our cities and towns, but break the morale of our people and prevent us from developing a proper defence and mobilizing our man power and armaments.
That is what I said on March 24, 1938, but nothing has been done. What has been done to protect the civilian population in Canada from awful air raids? One of these days there will be a rude awakening in this country. Hon. members sit in' this chamber and listen to one or two speeches by their leaders, and then all they do is say, "me too." So far as they are concerned, the people can continue to suffer or lack the security which is better than opulence. I consider that hon. gentlemen opposite and in other corners, who are not here to-night are not doing their duty.
I do not want to criticize them or anyone because I am sometimes away myself. My point is that they do not realize the importance and magnitude of this question of national defence, and our lack of any security whatever. Security is more important than social credit or all the trade treaties and trade pacts put together. We have had many of these trade pacts, but what is supposed to be their function? It was thought that when we had trade pacts and favoured nation treaties in twenty-six countries, they would lead to peace, but they have led toward more strife and war than to peace.
The government has not yet made a definite announcement as to the security of Canada. As far as I can see, the defences of Canada are where they were in 1812. We are com-
.2456
Foreign Policy-Mr. Church

pletely dependent upon the mother country for our defence in the air, on the land or on the sea, just as we were then. Canada is not going to be talked out of the British empire.
If Canada could have been talked out of the British empire, it would have been talked out long ago by the pacifists both in and out of this house. Canada will have to be fought out of the British empire. We have these pacifists and foreign commentators engaged by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, one of the most mischievous institutions we have, allowing attacks on Mr. Chamberlain and Great Britain and her foreign policies. Why should these foreigners and commentators and pacifists be engaged in debates or be allowed to link up different radio stations for an attack on Mr. Chamberlain and the British empire?
What is the British empire for? The British empire does not want war. Great Britain does not want war. She is trustee for the peace of the world. Great Britain protects Quebec and the maritimes, and indeed, all Canada. Were it not for the protection of Great Britain, Quebec, the maritimes and eastern Canada could be blotted out in twenty-four hours by the supremacy of the dictators in the air. That is what might have happened if they had decided to go west instead of east. Germany with her modern war preparations started as a small country and built up a vaster Germany through armaments obtained by loans from the democracies. While Germany was at war, she was surrounded by pacifist neighbours. Peace was on the lips of her statesmen, but war was in the hearts of the minorities. War has been the moral custom of Prussia from the time she was a petty state until the time she was a powerful empire. To-day she plans cruelly, deliberately, ruthlessly and with terrible ferocity; she executes her plans and policy at the appointed time and hour, after the victims have been lulled cleverly into a false sense of security. She cleverly isolates the wells of public opinion by crafty, poisonous publicity to the point of making the attacked appear in the eyes of the world as the aggressor. That is what happened in the case of Czechoslovakia.
Germany has an air supremacy of three to one. France with 40,000,000 people cannot stand against an invasion by 120,000,000 Germans and Italians, and now Spain is with the dictators as well. Dictators have lined up in southwest Europe 40,000,000 more against France. They have a supremacy in the air of three to one; they have a supremacy in man power, and they claim a supremacy in military services. They claim to be superior to all other people of the world in their

readiness to sacrifice. Pitt faced in the Napoleonic wars a similar state of affairs to that which England has to face in 1939. In 1803 Pitt, who strove for peace, was up against a dictator, Napoleon, and at that time he said that England must adopt precautions which were formerly thought unnecessary.
In my opinion this House of Commons should have before it all the telegrams, all the agreements and all the orders in council which I asked for last Monday. When this question was called the Speaker said, ' dropped." But the public are not going to drop this. Mr. Chamberlain laid all his cards on the table, and all the papers I asked for last fall. He rose in his place in the house and gave the details and defects of the defences of London. He told the people how Germany was three to one as far as air force was concerned, and that Britain would have been destroyed owing to the inadequacy of London's defences. They started digging trenches in the parks, but the people knew all the facts.
What have we in this country? On the fifty-sixth day of this session we have long statements made about peace and foreign affairs, and no clarity or a plain statement as to where Canada stands. One would almost think Canada's defence policy was the reading of speeches and documents and statements, and the making of trade agreements; that the pen is mightier than the sword. We shall have to go over all this again. Imagine what the soldiers with the memories of 1914 to 1918 will think! Munich was brought about by the pacifists and by the isolationist policy of this government. The pacifists in England persuaded Ramsay MacDonald to scrap the finest army, navy and air force in the world, with the result that an unarmed Britain simply invited invasion. The dominions, after all is said and done, have been somewhat of a drag on the mother country for the past twenty years since the great war.
Mr. Chamberlain, the Prime Minister of Great Britain, in his unforgettable radio speech before the final conference in Munich, said:
How horrible, fantastic, incredible it is that we should be digging trenches and fitting gas masks because of a quarrel in a far-away
It seems still more impossible that a quarrel which is already settled in principle should be the subject of war.
However much one may sympathize with a small nation confronted by a big and powerful nation, we cannot in all circumstances undertake to involve the whole British Empire m a war simply on that account.
If we have to fight, it must be on larger issues than that.
I am myself a man of peace to the depths of my soul. Armed conflict between nations is a nightmare to me.

Chamberlain was in command on the bridge, and it devolved upon him to begin to repair all the damage that had been done by the pacifists and which brought about Munich. Chamberlain is on the bridge for weeks, twenty-four hours a day, but it is recognized now that his appeasement policy has failed. Canada stands to-day at the parting of the ways. So far as Canada is concerned, all we have done has been to make a series of international treaties, pacts and agreements, and we are now giving privileges to Germany under the most favoured nation clause. We have a trade agreement with Germany. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, we should withdraw our trade envoys from Germany. Why should Germany be favoured with a trade treaty after the way in which she has been acting since the great war? Why was Germany singled out for such favours or an agreement? We should have taught them a lesson long ago. The United States raised her tariffs against Germany as a penalty of displeasure. The United States is using the weapon of the tariff to show its disbelief in the frightful policy of Germany.
It is deplorable that the League of Nations has done more to promote strife than peace. The league now lies in ruins, and it has left Britain the goat, alone with France, against the dictators. The pacifists have brought about Munich and all it stood for.
It was deplorable that in order to please the United States in 1922 we drove Japan into Germany's arms. Japan had been our loyal and dependable ally for twenty years, and with the exception of France was of more value to Britain than any other nation.
By the policy practised at Ottawa in passing sanctions against Italy, and then turning right-about-face and revoking them, we drove Italy into the German orbit. Had Britain not been engaged in a quarrel with Italy, Germany would not have violated the treaty of Versailles and made it a scrap of paper and crossed the Rhine. It would not have captured Austria, gone on to Czechoslovakia and now be going on to the Black Sea and making a dash also for the Baltic.
_ The duty of Canada is to notify Britain immediately that she stands behind her and will cooperate with her, place all her power and all her natural resources behind Great Britain and her allies to the utmost of our strength and _ capacity, that she will stand with the empire to resist any further aggression by Germany and the dictators.
The statute of Westminster is largely to blame for a great deal of our trouble to-day. One of its provisions is that each dominion is made responsible for its own defence.
Foreign Policy-Mr. Church
Canada is a dominion and has no defence. New Zealand and Australia would not agree to that provision, and only a few weeks ago I read out to the house six or eight clauses which Australia and New Zealand would not adhere to or bind themselves to. These two dominions are cooperating with Great Britain against the dictators more than Canada is.
I believe that the Ontario legislature represents public opinion in this country better than does this honourable house. They passed a resolution that they were loyal to Great Britain, and the resolution called for immediate action by the component parts of Canada in support of the British government in the present international crisis, and for mobilization of wealth and man power. There are to-day six thousand men from my own city lying buried in Flanders, but most of all in glorious France, that country towards whom the eyes of the whole civilized world were turned in the great war. The suffering and tribulations which France endured in the great war for civilization and liberty will live in history as an example of the most sublime heroism.
I believe that by a system of education properly undertaken, the youth of the province of Quebec would learn to see what Britain stands for. Sixty thousand of our glorious dead lie in France where they sleep their last sleep. That land of France is forever sacred to us, and we can never forget our glorious ally Iby whose side they fought. What we need in this country to-day is leadership in government, and that all parties in this house should unite for a maximum of unity and a minimum of discord. The people of the province of Quebec by leadership will see that they have more to fear from dictators, whose warships, with their powerful pompom guns may come up the St. Lawrence, fire a few hundreds of miles inland to the extent of their range and destroy the entire countryside.
I deplore the attacks that have been made by some of the Canadian French press on Britain and her leadership and also on a beloved member of this house and a very fine citizen of this country, the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). I believe that his heart is always for freedom and with Britain. We all know him to be a great Canadian and that he is assisting the leader of the government and the leader of the opposition in trying to bring about unity in this country.
I think the Ontario legislature did a very fine thing when they passed a resolution the other day for the mobilization of Canada's wealth and man power for the defence of freedom and liberty in the event of a future war. Britain has not asked Canada for any
Foreign Policy-Mr. Church

contribution, tout she does expect that Canada will give her moral support and let the dictators know that the dominions are safe and sound, if needed. Speaking in the Ontario legislature on the resolution, Doctor Aurelien Belanger of Prescott, whose ancestor came to Canada in one of Champlain's ships and married a French girl at Quebec in 1642, said:
We are loyal because we are grateful. We are loyal because we think our interests are tied to Great Britain. We are loyal because we think the rights we enjoy are better guaranteed under the British flag than under any other allegiance. We are loyal, I say, speaking for the majority, because we are a part of the British Empire.
The resolution, which was passed unanimously, reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government of Ontario should take cognizance of the fact that the present international crisis in Europe calls for immediate action on the part of the component parts of the British Empire, in support of any action which it may be necessary for the imperial government to take.
And that this legislative assembly of Ontario hereby petitions the federal parliament of Canada, now in session, to immediately pass legislation providing that in the event of a war emergency, the wealth and man power of Canada shall be mobilized by proclamation of the governor general in council, for the duration of the war, in defence of our free institutions.
All leaders, and the whole legislature, are to be congratulated upon their wisdom and patriotism.
If democracies are to be preserved, Canada must do its part. Do we realize what the weakness of last September meant to Canada? Canada must let the dictators know that Canada will do its duty as it did in 1914. The youth of the country do not want to fight for such shams as the League of Nations, or for paper sanctions, or for "war to end war," or against mere fascism or communism imposed on some foreign countries three thousand miles away from Canada; they will fight-with leadership-for God and king and country, if the government will give them the facts and let them know. If they have the real facts and it is found necessary for the defence of the country I believe they will do what they did in 1914, if they have leadership and know what Britain stands for. After all is said and done, as the eleventh Psalm, verse 3, puts it: "If the foundations be destroyed, what then shall the righteous do?" And what will the people of Canada do if their foundations are destroyed, as they may be destroyed by a visit of the dictators here? As Adam Smith said, security is better than opulence.
There has been, in my opinion, a lack of prudence and wisdom in the part which 
Canada has been playing in foreign affairs since the great war. It has been a policy of drift, of inaction, of coma, of inertia, of doubt and fear, of straddling the fence. Canada's foreign policy has lost in eighteen years much that was won by the valour of Canadian soldiers. We renounced the great position we held in the eyes of Great Britain, the dominions and the world, won at great loss and cost by our armies in the fields. We have thrown all these away and have relied on conferences, pacts, protocols, the League of Nations and all kinds of provocative pacifism such as led Britain to disarm. Courage, prudence and leadership are the needs of to-day for those who control our affairs in Canada. There is too much talk of small trade advantages and a general contempt for security. Security is disregarded and trade agreements are relied on for defence, although everyone who knows the facts realizes that in the end the lack of defence will lead to war and the sacrifice of not only the external but the internal safety of the country. The people of England are sick and tired of the weak surrender which was made by the socialist government, and they are rearming for the good of civilization. When they are fully armed we shall see the end of dictators.
The other day Lord Baldwin made a speech at Worcester, in which he said:
While I believe all that, I know that unless the will to peace exists in the hearts and souls of all the leaders in Europe, there may come a time when war will be inevitable. But if that time comes, I know this . . . Whether it be long or short, there can be but one result; and this country with a cause to fight for, the liberty of the human spirit, will fight with a unanimity of all classes and all ranks that has never been seen in any war that has yet taken place.
No one is better entitled to speak than Lord Baldwin; no one is better entitled to make that declaration of faith. But why wait for war? Can we not have to-day unanimity of all classes and all ranks in Canada in conjunction with Britain so that we shall be prepared? Any Canadian defence policy is inseparable from empire defence. We must give full cooperation and support to the British army, navy and air force in any plan we have for cooperation for defence purposes.
Reference was made to the disarmed neutrality which Canada has been practising. It is a luxury which no country can permit itself in the neighbourhood of the great aggressor; for there is still the possibility to be considered of Herr Hitler or one of the dictators with designs on Canada's natural resources coming over here. It is not only a possibility but a probability. The other day we had

Foreign Policy-Mr. Pelletier
some mysterious visitors here looking over our lumber. A year ago there was discussion about German aeroplanes flying over Canada. They know a great deal more about Canada than a good many Canadians; they know more than many absentee members of this house, and some day there may be a rude awakening.
I hope that the British government will tell Germany once and for all that so far as giving them back the colonies is concerned, that is out of the question.
Reference has been made here to the people of the United States. It is of tremendous importance to the people of this country to be on good terms with them, and we thank them for all they have done. But remember they have enough to do to look after their own country. I doubt if, were they attacked, they could do anything further. As to the policy of that country, the United States always speaks with two voices. One is the president's voice, the other is the voice of congress. Under the terms of the Johnson act, which is binding upon the president, they cannot give any equipment or supplies for the armies of the allies; and under the Ludlow resolution they are completely out of foreign commitments, they are back to the days of Andrew Jackson and George Washington, whose object was to keep out of all wars the world over, Canada included. We cannot depend upon them for protection. I say this while realizing it is of the utmost importance that we have their cooperation and goodwill, and we rejoice at the recent meeting of the Prime Minister of this country with the president, when they told the dictators a few things which commended themselves to the wisdom and judgment of the country.
Nevertheless, in attempting to please the United States, we can see what has happened since 1920. By the treaty of Washington the empire lost its Japanese ally. In 1926 the government of the day, thinking the British empire was too strong, committed the imperial conference to the statute of Westminster. Friendship with the United States is obviously of great importance to the people of Canada, but it is like anything else worth having-more likely to be obtained by taking a firm line than by giving way. on every occasion. For example, several states of the union owe British investors a large sum of money, but successive governments have refused to raise the issue for fear of wounding United States susceptibilities. In fact there are times when it seems that the British foreign policy is more careful of the United States than of British security. On the other hand numerous attacks were made by United States newspapers on Mr. Chamberlain because of the Munich treaty. I have been able to find only three or four newspapers which did not attack Britain and Chamberlain on that issue. I believe that the time has come when we shall have to rely, as we did in 1812, on Britain for protection. I see a cartoon here which puts it bluntly:
Uncle Sam:	If anything should happen to
John Bull it will be a case of me helping you.
Jack Canuck:	Yep, an' may Heaven help
us both.
It is a picture of our old friend Uncle Sam talking to Jack Canuck, and Jack says, "If we are going to depend on you, we are down and out," or in the words of the cartoon, "Heaven help us both." Both are protected by Britain from the dictators.
The Prime Minister was not slow to tell the people of the United States what he would do. He would never allow an enemy to go through the dominion to invade the United States. What about helping Britain? The Prime Minister proclaims Canada's responsibility for her own protection.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As I rise to take part in this serious and important debate, I do so with the realization that the statements made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) on Monday, March 20, must now seem like a dim and faraway nightmare to certain members of this house whom the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) often has called "troubles close at home." On that date he said this:
If ever there were a prospect of an aggressor launching an attack on Britain, with bombers raining death on London, I have no doubt what the decision of the Canadian people and parliament would be.
Of course, since that time we know what that statement caused. It caused a great deal of discussion in the legislature of Ontario, which was immediately replied to by some demonstration or another in the legislative assembly of Quebec. I would point out to the Prime Minister that he did not say that if there was an aggressor raining bombs on Great Britain, Canada would go to her assistance. He said simply that if there were even a prospect of an aggressor launching an attack on Great Britain, he had no doubt what the decision of the Canadian people and parliament would be. It is for that reason I point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that to-day's attitude on the part of the Prime Minister is so complete a reversal that it must have brought a great deal of pleasure to those hon. members
Foreign Policy-Mr. Pelletier

to whom I have referred as called by the Minister of Justice his "little troubles very close at home."
I believe that the Prime Minister's speech to-day, because of its length and importance, is very hard to digest and could not be commented upon satisfactorily without due consideration and proper study. I listened carefully to the Prime Minister and was struck with the departure in Canada's foreign policy as he announced it to-day. He said that this government is not prepared to commit this country by new and unspecified commitments operating under conditions which cannot now be foreseen. With that statement I quite agree, but I am sure that the interpretation which will be put upon his speech, and which he has conveyed to the house, is that between Canada and the United States there has been brought about a closer rapprochement with an evident trend away from Great Britain. I am sure that interpretation will be placed on the Prime Minister's statement, and because I take a realistic view of the situation I believe he was quite right in assuming that position. As I say, however, I feel sure that interpretation will be given his speech-a rapprochement to the United States rather than to Great Britain. For example, after stating that the government is not prepared to commit the country by new and unspecified commitments operating under conditions which cannot now be foreseen, he proceeded to make it clear that so far as Canada was concerned everything in our power would be done to prevent the dominion from allowing any aggressor ever to approach the territorial boundaries of the United States.
Consider what that means. Suppose Belgium were to say, "We will not allow any aggressor to cross our territory in order to attack France;" that would be analogous to what the Prime Minister stated-that Canada would not permit any aggressor to cross Canadian soil in order to reach the United States. How can that be interpreted other than as a closer rapprochement to the United States and a departure from the former desire to have the British people believe that Canada was as close to Great Britain as she is to the United States. I say this without disloyalty and because I firmly believe that it is the interpretation which must be put upon the statements of the Prime Minister to-day, because the action he has taken is self-evident. Perhaps the rest of the world will view his speech as I have done.
The Prime Minister began by referring to the crisis that came to a head in Munich last year, and he went on to survey the posi-

tion of the various nations at that time. Perhaps what I shall say will be the first note of discord which so far has been introduced into the debate, but I firmly believe that I am not alone in the view I am about to express. Indeed, I will substantiate my statements with the views of others who are far greater than I am. We find that the Prime Minister absolved Mr. Chamberlain completely of blame for what happened at Munich. He said he was glad that Mr. Chamberlain had been able to preserve the peace of the world. With that statement I agree entirely. Moreover, I agree that there was no sound reason why Great Britain should go to war at that time. Much as I regret the unhappy plight of certain central European countries, nevertheless I ask, what earthly use would have been served if thousands of lives had been sacrificed in warfare? Have we such an intense fellow feeling for other people that we should play the knight in shining armour and rush off to the assistance of all and sundry who find themselves in difficulties for the time being? If that is so, what are the people of Czechoslovakia suffering to-day that the people of China are not called upon to suffer?
I could mention other examples. There are dozens of other peoples who are suffering under aggressor nations. Was it for the Prime Minister of Great Britain, supported by the Prime Minister of Canada, to rush off, and as I say, play the knight in shining armour on behalf of all these countries that are suffering to-day in central Europe? Should that course have been followed simply on sentimental grounds, because those peoples happen to have the same ideals that we hold with respect to democracy? It would have been ridiculous and I do not think anything of the sort could have been done. Geographically we could not do it; we are so far removed from that theatre of war that it would not have been possible.
The point I want to make is this. I do not believe that Mr. Chamberlain ever had any intention of going to war even at the time of the Czechoslovak crisis. If anyone thinks he had, it is easy to go back, over the record and find a dozen reasons why such an intention, if he had it, should have been carried into practice prior to that time. Let us look at the history of Hitler's regime and try to find situations similar to that in which Czechoslovakia found itself in September of last year. Going over that record this is what we find in chronological order:
October 14, 1933-Hitler announces Germany's withdrawal from the League of Nations and world disarmament conference.

September 29-Four-power conference in Munich averts threatened European war by agreeing to give Sudetenland to Germany; later conferences gave parts of Czecho-Slovakia to Poland and Hungary.
October 1-Nazi troops cross Czech frontier; Chamberlain and Hitler sign statement never to fight again.
October 29-Hitler's deputy says Germany will claim all pre-war colonies-a total area of J .127.0951 square miles including former German East Africa, Southwest Africa, Togoland, five groups of Pacific ocean islands.
November 2-Germany and Italian foreign ministers at Vienna award more Czechoslovak territory to Hungary.

Since that time Memel has become German territory.
Does anyone mean to tell me that in what I have related there were not several instances of events that might have caused the same kind of crisis which occurred in Czechoslovakia last September; which meant just as much to Great Britain as did the impending fall of Czechoslovakia? The point I should like to make is this: I believe that the Prime Minister knew definitely during the last crisis in September that there was not going to be any

war, and that Herr Hitler never had any intention of going to war. There was no reason I could see, simply the desire on his part to play the shining knight and to rush off and assist some central European country which might happen to have a democratic tendency, the same as Great Britain.
Now we say to ourselves, is this march likely to continue? I simply have to pick up to-night's paper and find this; German army reported along Polish border. It might simply be said that this army has been massed there to scare, or to attempt to blackmail certain negotiations going on at the present time in Europe. Nevertheless no one can make me believe that the Prime Minister of Great Britain through his foreign office and secret service was so poorly informed as not to know two weeks ahead of time what was going to happen in Europe. I feel sure they are in a position, and always have been, to foresee events not merely two weeks ahead of time but a great many months ahead, because that has been British policy ever since Great Britain has been the mighty power she is to-day. They believe in being informed; they plan ahead of time knowing full well the consequences of their plans, and seek to achieve their goal by whatever means they may find it necessary to use. This bears out the belief I have that it was never the intention of the Prime Minister of Great Britain to go to war. That is why I say the remarks I have made this evening might strike some note of discord in the harmony we have had in this house to-day. But it is a shameful thing, a despicable thing, to play with the feelings of the people and to use an imaginary situation to build up an atmosphere to support a vast rearmament program either in this country or in Great Britain.
What happened here? We heard the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) time and time again complain bitterly that he was not called in during the crisis, that the Prime Minister had not called him in at the time when the state of affairs in Europe appeared so serious. The answer simply is that the Prime Minister knew there was not going to be any war, and there was no need to call in the leaders of the various parties. Why call in the leaders when you know definitely there is not going to be any war? I find the attitude of the leader of the opposition rather unusual, because his channels of information should be at least as good as mine.
An hon. MEMBER; What do you suggest?

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The record is there. It clearly shows that a series of things such as happened in Czechoslovakia happened over a
Foreign Policy-Mr. Pelletier

period of time. What happened in Spain, for instance? What about the non-intervention pact? Why was it not equally right to fight for democracy elsewhere as to fight for democracy in Czechoslovakia? The British Prime Minister made it quite clear that the role Great Britain played was simply that of mediator, and that the only commitment Great Britain had in Europe was simply to support France in case France found it necessary to send troops to help Czechoslovakia. There was no direct commitment on the part of Great Britain; he was acting simply and solely as mediator in that dispute. Undoubtedly his services might have been required; but inasmuch as he knew ahead of time exactly what the outcome would be, why was it necessary to play upon the fears of the people to support a rearmament program? That is exactly what happened. Great Britain was not ready at that time to engage in war, according to various declarations made in the British House of Commons, but was it right that they should use an excuse of that kind to build up armaments? Did anyone ever hear or see anything more ridiculous than the digging of trenches in Hyde park? What good would they be in case bombers rained death on the city of London? None at all, of course. In my opinion it was a part of that build-up undertaken to stir up the spirit of the British people to support an armament program, and a much needed one.
I do not believe it is necessary to do things like that. The leaders both in this country and in Great Britain should have more faith in the loyalty of the people. They should tell them what is necessary; simply say, "We need to defend ourselves; we do not know how far these people are going in Europe, we need to arm ourselves to protect ourselves"; and I believe the people of this country and of Great Britain would have been loyal enough to support their leaders to the utmost of their ability. And the Canadian people would have agreed to place their resources at the disposal of this country in order to defend and protect our shores.
I said I would substantiate my statement by statements made by leaders in other countries. One man whom the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), for example, often wants to quote, who, I think, is well known as a solid Britisher, John Maynard Keynes, gives his view quite clearly. This is what he wrote in The New Statesman and Nation of October 8, 1938, shortly after the crisis:
The Prime Minister was never preparing for the actuality of war. The total omission of any referenee_ even to the possibility of military action by this country in the correspondence published in the white paper, the avoidance

of conversations with Russia, the reluctance and extraordinary delay in ordering the mobilization of the fleet are not consistent with any other explanation. Neither the Prime Minister nor Herr Hitler ever intended for one moment that the play acting should devolve into reality. For it would be a mistake to attribute extreme carelessness to the one or insanity to the other of these two astute politicians. The actual course of events has been dictated by the fact that the objectives of Herr Hitler and Mr. Chamberlain were not different, but the same;
He concludes the article by saying:
The Prime Minister thinks it a small price to pay and can swallow with a good conscience a week's play acting, beginning with gas masks and ending with bouquets, even if it involved a brief moment of harsh plucking at mothers' heartstrings.
The record is there, and the record is clear. What happened during the September crisis was a thing which has occurred time and time again. Did Great Britain think of going to war on the other occasions? Of course not. Why, therefore, should she have departed from her policy because of Czechoslovakia? The Czech people are just as human as the people of China or of Ethiopia, whose countries were members of the League of Nations. But what was the truth? The truth was that Great Britain was not prepared at that time to put up the front which she would have done under different circumstances. I criticize both the Prime Minister of Great Britain and the Prime Minister of this country for not telling their people the truth of the matter, because I know full well that they can rely on the loyalty of the people they govern.
There is another aspect of the case which I think is interesting. Time and again, on many occasions, the Prime Minister has stated that a policy of trade agreements was just as great a defence against war as any armaments that we might build.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: When? Get down to the facts.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will put it in this way, that the Prime Minister believes firmly that he is contributing to the cause of peace when he is entering into trade agreements with other nations. I believe that in expressing it in that way I am actually conveying the impression the Prime Minister has given the house from time to time. I believe that for various reasons that is quite true concerning the United States trade agreement. I believe it could be called a natural agreement, because the peoples of these two countries are similar in habits. They live closely together, and their customs are very much the same. I believe it could be labeled a natural agreement because of the geographical location which we enjoy on the north American

Foreign Policy-Mr. Pelletier
continent. Because of this I believe the trade agreement between the United States of America and Canada does enhance our interests in each other, and thereby strengthens the stand we have taken to-day, which is a closer rapprochement to the United States of America, made quite clear by the policy enuniciated to-day by the Prime Minister himself.
However, there is something else we must consider in connection with various trade agreements. It is this, that, distinctly different from the kind of trade agreement which we recently concluded with the United States are other agreements which we have concluded with other nations far removed from our own country. I have no doubt those agreements are quite necessary. I know that once in a while the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) goes on pilgrimages to secure new markets. But the way in which things are going to-day under our present economic set-up and financial system, it does not make much difference to him where he finds those markets, so long as they are markets for the Canadian people. That is where in my opinion the danger creeps in, because every time a country is able to secure a market, that market is secured only after there has been intensely heated international competition for it. Surely it is not conducive to harmony among nations.
While at the moment I do not recall the exact words of the late President Wilson, I believe he did say something to the effect that the seeds of war are sown in the hotbed of heated and intense international commercial competition. That should be evident to all, because when we secure a market we must necessarily take it away from somebody else who is trying to secure that same market.
What is the result? The result is that the nation which formerly supplied that market and is no longer able to do so is going to adopt new ways and means to get back the market it had originally. Its action may take the form of subsidies to industries. That was done in Japan, and what happened? The countries of the world were forced to erect tariff barriers to keep out Japanese goods, to keep them from competing with the goods made in those respective countries. That was done because Japan had adopted the method of subsidizing its manufacturers so that they could compete in the world markets.
There are other ways of securing markets which nations have lost. One of them is, of course, by lowering the standard of living in the country affected, by bringing about a reduction of wage levels of the workers in that country. That is done in various countries.
We say that we cannot compete with such and such a nation because our standard of living and our wage level are higher than they are elsewhere. But the important point to remember is that those countries used the method of lowering the standard of living of their own people to regain markets.
Then, there is another way of doing it- and in my opinion this is the most horrible of them all. When nations find that they are surrounded, and cannot find the markets they require, what do they do? Too often they resort to force of arms. That has been so on many occasions, and I am sure that if the true history of past wars could be told we would find at the bottom of them the same excuse, namely intense international competition for markets.
I see you are getting restless, Mr. Speaker. I realize it is after eleven o'clock, but I have only a few more words and, with the consent of the house, I should like to conclude.
Some lion. MEMBERS: Go on.

speechtext: Make up your suggestion.

speechtext: I shall. The Prime Minister to-day referred in a rather sarcastic vein when he said that he resented-I am not quite sure I have the word at the moment- that he objected strongly to the type of newspapers which carried scare head-lines across the country.

speechtext: My hon. friend ought to be very careful what he says, and should not talk of things he does not know anything about.

subsubtopic: FOREIGN POLICY-STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I beg to differ with the right hon. gentleman. That is the impression which I got. I do not think I am imputing motives to anyone. The Prime Minister did
Foreign Policy-Mr. Pelletier

make some sort of statement resenting the type of scare propaganda which might go on from time to time in this country. Now, I have said it was done for the purpose of increasing their circulation. Perhaps I should not have said that, because I do agree that the right hon. gentleman did not say it, himself. Nevertheless there is something in what I said. May I just point out that even in his own telegram congratulating the right hon. the Prime Minister of Great Britain, this is the type of words he used: "On the very brink of chaos". That is one of his expressions. Picture how that would sound if it were read from the headlines of various newspapers across Canada. The Prime Minister has used those words. But that is not all; here is another expression he used: "With passions flaming"-and he was referring, of coui'se, to the passions of the people in European countries. What would the newspapers do with those very words contained in his own telegram of congratulations? What would they with those words, if they did not arouse the feeling of the people of Canada? Then, farther on, he referred to 'armies marching"

again emphasizing the danger of the situation, and attempting to show that the danger was great and that we have need to prepare ourselves.
In conclusion, I say that I believe in the loyalty of the Canadian people-perhaps even to a greater degree, if that is possible, than does the Prime Minister himself. I believe the proper attitude to take would have been to tell the people what the situation was, and not to try to scare them into supporting an armament program, simply because they are not prepared to face the eventualities of the time.
We do need armaments, and I believe this country is going to provide them. I believe, too, that we should provide defence armament, for defence purposes, before we do anything else. I say that so far as Canada's attitude is concerned, I approve the stand taken to-day by the Prime Minister when he referred to building up more armaments, defending our own country, having a stronger alliance and closer relationship with the United States and promising Great Britain that we shall do all in our power to help by offering the raw materials and resources at our command, thereby fulfilling our obligations.
On motion of Mr. Lapointe (Quebec East) the debate was adjourned.
It being ten minutes after eleven o'clock, the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
